title: Find the tag that names you
allegory: K-composition is a two-host party trick: the first host writes on every guest's tag who stood just before them, and the second host finds 'whoever came after Alice' by searching those tags, not the guests themselves.
map: host 1 writes 'after Alice' on Bob's tag
the previous-token head writes token A's identity into the residual stream at position A+1
host 2 searches the tags for 'after Alice'
the induction head's keys read that written subspace: K-composition
host 2 asks using Alice's own name
the query comes from the current token's embedding
calling out the name of the guest wearing that tag
the induction head's OV circuit copies B to the logits

chapters.name: One head can't
arrows: finds the old Harry... then what?

cap.1: Seen 'Harry Potter' once, then 'Harry' again? You'd guess 'Potter'. But one attention step can find the earlier Harry, not the word that came after it.
cap.2: Induction: in '... A B ... A', predict B. One head can match A to earlier A's, but the key at B's position knows nothing about the A before it. Something must put that there first.
cap.3: At B's position the residual stream holds only B's embedding and position, so no single-layer QK can select 'the position after A'. A prior head must move A forward one position.

cap.1: At a party, host one walks down the line and writes on each guest's tag who stood just before them. Bob's tag now says: after Alice.
cap.2: Layer 0's previous-token head does exactly this: at every position it writes the previous token's identity into the residual stream. B's position now carries 'A came before me'.
cap.3: The prev-token head (0.7 in ARENA's two-layer attention-only model) attends from i to i−1, and its OV writes token[i−1] into a subspace of the residual stream at i.

cap.1: Later, Alice speaks again. Host two scans the tags for 'after Alice', finds Bob, and calls out 'Bob!'. It searched the tags, not the guests.
cap.2: Layer 1's induction head asks with the current token (A). Its keys read the tag the first head wrote, so it attends to B's position, then copies B to the output.
cap.3: K-composition: the induction head's keys read the subspace the prev-token head wrote, its query reads the current token's embedding, and its OV circuit copies B to the logits.

cap.1: Chain the two hosts' rules into one table: for each name host two hears, which tag does it pick? In a working pair, every name picks the tag with its own name.
cap.2: Multiply the layer-1 head's QK matrix by the layer-0 head's OV matrix, with embeddings on both ends. The exercise builds this K-comp circuit and checks its diagonal.
cap.3: W_Eᵀ W_QK^1.4 W_OV^0.7 W_E scores 'query token q attends where the previous token was k'. Induction needs it diagonal-dominant; top_1_acc measures that.

chapters.name: The quiet host
chapters.verdict: A head that only writes tags looks idle until you remove it.

cap.1: Host one never calls out a name, so if you only credit whoever shouts, host one looks useless. Send host one home and the whole trick stops working.
cap.2: Direct logit attribution only sees each head's direct effect on the logits. The previous-token head's effect is entirely indirect, so DLA misses it; zero-ablating it breaks induction.
cap.3: DLA measures only the direct path; K-composition contributions are indirect by construction. Causal checks (zero-ablating one head at a time, watching second-half loss) are required.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Two small rules compose into an algorithm
Read the circuit from weights alone

cap.1: Big abilities are often small rules handed along: one head writes a tag, another reads it. Spotting these hand-offs is how you understand what a model is doing.
cap.2: K-composition is how induction heads work, and Olsson et al. (2022) tied induction heads to in-context learning. Composition scores find such head pairs from the weights.
cap.3: Composition through the residual stream is the unit of circuit analysis: finding K- and Q-composition edges turns a list of heads into a mechanism you can test, ablate or steer.

coda.title: Where does the second ' Harry' look? Dial the tag writer and the tag reader

params.label: host 1: how clearly it writes tags
host 2: how hard its keys read tags

readouts.label: attention from the last ' Harry' to ' Potter'
induction guess
readouts.f: softmax([0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0].map(m => gain*tag*m))[2] > 0.5 ? ' Potter' : 'no idea: attention is spread out'

caption.1: Host one starts switched off, as if removed: attention is spread flat, however hard host two reads. Raise the tag writer and watch it lock onto ' Potter'.
caption.2: Attention from the second ' Harry' is softmax of reader × writer on the one position whose tag says Harry. Composition is a product: if either head gives zero, induction fails.
caption.3: The K-comp term is W_QK of the later head applied to the earlier head's OV write. Zero-ablate the prev-token head (writer = 0) and the induction stripe collapses to uniform.

where_else: Induction heads: the previous-token head writes, the induction head's keys read
IOI's circuit: later heads read what earlier heads wrote, through Q- and K-composition
Any system where one stage labels items so a later stage can search by label, like a database index
Composition scores: spotting which head pairs talk, from weights alone

hamming.what: A later attention head builds its keys from what an earlier head wrote into the residual stream, so the two heads act as one algorithm.
hamming.when: Whenever a behaviour needs information that isn't at a position yet, like 'the token after the last copy of me' in induction.
hamming.why: A single head can only match what is already at each position; composition lets two layers express searches neither head could do alone.
